chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halby, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the Prayer of Fear. He said: The Imam stands, and a group of his companions comes and stands behind him, while another group faces the enemy. The Imam prays one Rak'ah with them. Then he stands, and they stand with him, so he represents them standing, and they pray the second Rak'ah. Then some of them greet each other with Salaam, and then they disperse. They stand in the place of their companions, and the others come and stand behind the Imam. The Imam prays the second Rak'ah with them. Then the Imam sits, and they stand and pray another Rak'ah. Then he greets them, and they disperse by his greeting.

He said: And in the Maghrib prayer, it is similar to that. The Imam stands, and a group comes and stands behind him. Then he prays one Rak'ah with them. Then he stands, and they stand, so the Imam represents them standing, and they pray the two Rak'ahs. They perform Tashahhud, and some of them greet each other. Then they disperse, stand in the place of their companions, and the others come and stand behind the Imam. He prays one Rak'ah with them, reciting therein. Then he sits and performs Tashahhud. Then he stands, and they stand with him, and he prays another Rak'ah with them. Then he sits, and they stand and complete another Rak'ah. Then he greets them.
ai.seo_question: How is the Prayer of Fear (Salat al-Khawf) performed according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi provides a detailed procedural account of Salat al-Khawf, illustrating the practical application of the Quranic concession for prayer during combat. It highlights the Imam's role in dividing the congregation into two groups to balance worship and vigilance, a method endorsed by Shia jurists as the primary mode for the Prophet and Imams. The text also extends this ruling to the Maghrib prayer, demonstrating the flexibility of the ritual structure under duress.
